intro: In this college you'll learn to talk about the weather and the four seasons, to compare things with comparatives and superlatives, to discuss climate change, to suggest getting a pet, and to talk about the nature you miss from home.

paragraphs.heading: Why the weather matters here
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme eighteen. Its title is [[De natuur is overal]], which means 'Nature is everywhere'. In the Netherlands the weather is the number one topic for small talk, so learning these words helps you in countless daily moments: at the bus stop, in the lift, with your neighbour over the fence. The most useful opening question is [[Wat voor weer is het vandaag?]], meaning 'What is the weather like today?'. A warm, very Dutch way to start a chat is [[Lekker weertje, he?]], a friendly 'Nice weather, isn't it?'. Let's gather the core words. The weather itself is [[het weer]]. The sun is [[de zon]], the rain is [[de regen]], the wind is [[de wind]], and snow is [[de sneeuw]]. A cloud is [[de wolk]]. Notice that many weather sentences use a little 'it', just like in English. So 'it is raining' is [[het regent]], 'it is snowing' is [[het sneeuwt]], and on a cold night 'it is freezing' is [[het vriest]]. For other weather you say [[het is]] plus a word, like [[het is zonnig]], meaning 'it is sunny', or [[het is koud]], 'it is cold'. I explain in English, but every Dutch phrase is spoken by a native voice, so repeat each one out loud after me.

paragraphs.heading: The four seasons
paragraphs.text: Now let's walk through the year. The word for a season is [[het seizoen]], and there are four of them. Spring is [[de lente]], summer is [[de zomer]], autumn is [[de herfst]], and winter is [[de winter]]. To say when something happens, use 'in' plus the season, like [[in de zomer]], meaning 'in summer', or [[in de winter]], 'in winter'. Here is a tip about real Dutch weather: it changes fast and it is often grey and wet, even in summer, so people carry a coat all year. In spring you will hear [[In de lente schijnt de zon vaker]], meaning 'in spring the sun shines more often'. In summer many Dutch people say [[In de zomer gaan we naar het strand]], 'in summer we go to the beach'. Autumn is famously windy, so a classic sentence is [[In de herfst waait het hard]], meaning 'in autumn the wind blows hard'. And in winter, [[In de winter sneeuwt het soms]], 'in winter it sometimes snows'. A lovely Dutch proverb captures their patient mood about weather: [[Na regen komt zonneschijn]], literally 'after rain comes sunshine', which really means that better times always follow the bad. Say it when a friend has a hard day; it sounds caring and very Dutch.

paragraphs.heading: Comparing things: warmer and warmest
paragraphs.text: Here comes the grammar of this theme, and it is wonderfully simple. To compare two things, you add '-er' to the adjective. So [[warm]], meaning 'warm', becomes [[warmer]], 'warmer'. To say 'than', you use the little word [[dan]]. For example: [[Vandaag is het warmer dan gisteren]], meaning 'Today it is warmer than yesterday'. To say something is the most of all, the superlative, you add '-st' and usually put [[het]] in front. So 'the warmest' is [[het warmst]]. You get a neat little ladder: [[warm]], then [[warmer]], then [[het warmst]]. Try it with another word: 'big' is [[groot]], 'bigger' is [[groter]], and 'the biggest' is [[het grootst]]. So you can say [[Een hond is groter dan een poes]], 'a dog is bigger than a cat'. Two important words are irregular, so just memorise them. 'Good' is [[goed]], but 'better' is [[beter]] and 'best' is [[het best]]. And 'much' is [[veel]], 'more' is [[meer]], 'most' is [[het meest]]. With long words ending in '-isch' you do not add '-er'; you use [[meer]] in front instead. Practise out loud: [[koud, kouder, het koudst]], meaning 'cold, colder, coldest'. This pattern will serve you everywhere.

paragraphs.heading: Climate change and steeds
paragraphs.text: Let's use those comparatives to talk about something serious: the climate. The climate is [[het klimaat]], and a simple, true sentence is [[Het klimaat verandert langzaam]], meaning 'the climate is changing slowly'. Now I want to teach you a small word that makes you sound really fluent: [[steeds]]. With a comparative it means 'more and more' or 'increasingly'. So [[De winters worden steeds warmer]] means 'the winters are getting warmer and warmer'. Hear the pattern: [[worden]] means 'are becoming', and [[steeds]] plus a comparative shows a growing change. You can say [[De zomers worden steeds droger]], 'the summers are getting drier and drier', or [[Het weer wordt steeds extremer]], 'the weather is getting more and more extreme'. This topic connects to a proud part of Dutch life: water. Much of the country lies below sea level, so the Dutch build sea walls called [[de dijken]] and drained lands called [[de polders]] to keep their feet dry. A famous saying is [[God schiep de wereld, maar de Nederlanders schiepen Nederland]], meaning 'God made the world, but the Dutch made the Netherlands'. When the forecast warns of bad weather, you might add a coat with [[Neem een jas mee, het wordt kouder]], 'take a coat, it is getting colder'.

paragraphs.heading: Pets and a friendly suggestion
paragraphs.text: Let's lighten the mood with pets, which are a big part of Dutch home life. A pet is [[het huisdier]]. The most common ones are a dog, [[de hond]], and a cat, for which there are two words: the formal [[de kat]] and the cosy, everyday [[de poes]]. You can say [[Wij hebben een hond en twee poezen]], meaning 'we have a dog and two cats'. Now here is the second piece of grammar: how to suggest doing something together. You use [[Zullen we]], meaning 'Shall we', then the rest, and the main verb goes right to the end in its basic form. So to propose getting a cat you say [[Zullen we een poes nemen?]], 'Shall we get a cat?'. The verb [[nemen]], 'to take' or 'to get', sits at the end. More examples: [[Zullen we de hond uitlaten?]] means 'Shall we walk the dog?', and [[Zullen we een wandeling maken?]] means 'Shall we go for a walk?'. To answer warmly, say [[Ja, goed idee!]], 'Yes, good idea!'. To decline gently, say [[Nee, liever niet]], meaning 'No, I'd rather not'. These little suggestions are gold for building friendships with neighbours and colleagues.

paragraphs.heading: Talking about nature you miss
paragraphs.text: Many of us miss the nature of the country we came from, and that is a beautiful thing to share. To say you miss something, use [[Ik mis]]. So you might say [[Ik mis de zon van mijn land]], meaning 'I miss the sun of my country', or [[Ik mis de bergen van thuis]], 'I miss the mountains from home'. To say what you love, use [[Ik hou van]], as in [[Ik hou van de natuur en van wandelen]], 'I love nature and walking'. A forest is [[het bos]], a great place for a walk. Now picture a real moment: it is a grey Saturday and your neighbour knocks. You say [[Hoi! Wat voor weer wordt het morgen?]], 'Hi! What will the weather be like tomorrow?'. She answers [[Morgen wordt het mooier weer]], 'tomorrow the weather will be nicer'. So you suggest [[Zullen we dan naar het bos gaan?]], 'Shall we go to the forest then?', and she smiles: [[Ja, goed idee!]]. You add [[Ik mis de natuur van mijn land]], and you have made a real connection. You can do this. [[Na regen komt zonneschijn]] — after rain comes sunshine. [[Heel goed gedaan, tot de volgende keer!]]
